items.title: Report: Airlines will face shortage of new airplanes until at least 2030
items.author: Stephen Pope
items.summary: Aviation analytics firm Cirium projects that aircraft delivery shortages will persist until at least 2030 due to ongoing supply chain and certification issues. Airlines are currently managing an 18,000-unit order backlog while keeping aging fleets in service longer.

brief.what: Aviation analytics firm Cirium reports that manufacturers will struggle to meet airline demand through 2030, citing engine availability, supplier bottlenecks, and certification delays. Consequently, the global fleet's average age has hit a record 15.2 years, with IATA noting a shortfall of over 5,000 expected fuel-efficient aircraft.
brief.who: Cirium, an aviation analytics company, and the International Air Transport Association (IATA), which represents global airlines.
brief.context: Airlines are facing increased operational costs, including higher maintenance spending and lease rates, as they retain older aircraft due to the inability of manufacturers to deliver new units.
brief.why: Cirium attributes the production constraints to supply chain failures and certification delays, while IATA highlights engine durability issues and spare-parts shortages as primary disruptors to airline operations.
brief.next: Cirium forecasts that the global passenger fleet will exceed 50,000 aircraft by 2045, though geopolitical and economic factors could influence these expansion plans.
